quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud and keep 'jam' and 'yet' clearly different.
quests.hint: 'jam' begins with [dʒ], a stop-then-hush; 'yet' begins with [j], a smooth glide. Only one of them has a closure.
quests.explanation: For [dʒ], the tongue blade touches the ridge and the air is released with voice. For [j], the tongue rises near the roof of the mouth but never touches it, and you glide into the vowel.
quests.textToSpeak: The jam isn't ready yet.
quests.phoneticHint: 'jam' [dʒæm] versus 'yam' [jæm], and 'yet' [jet] versus 'jet' [dʒet]. The sound in 'yet' starts like a very short [i].
commonMistakes: Saying 'jet' for 'yet' by adding a closure
Saying 'yam' for 'jam' by leaving out the closure

quests.instruction: Say it twice, slowly and then at natural speed, without blending [dʒ] vs [j].
quests.hint: 'German', 'just' and 'joined' begin with [dʒ]; 'your' and 'yoga' begin with [j].
quests.explanation: Switch quickly between a closure sound and a glide: [dʒ] stops the air first, [j] never does. Keep 'joined' and 'yoga' distinct even though they sit close together.
quests.textToSpeak: Your German teacher just joined our yoga class.
quests.phoneticHint: 'German' is [ˈdʒɜːrmən], 'yoga' is [ˈjoʊgə], and 'your' is [jɔːr]. In 'your', the glide flows straight into the vowel.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a friendly invitation.
quests.hint: [j] begins 'yesterday's' and 'you'; [dʒ] begins 'jazz' and 'joined'.
quests.explanation: In 'you should', the [j] glide is quick and light. In 'joined', the tongue makes contact and releases with voice. Hold the same contrast at natural speed.
quests.textToSpeak: Yesterday's jazz night was great; you should have joined us.
quests.phoneticHint: 'jazz' is [dʒæz], 'joined' is [dʒɔɪnd], 'yesterday's' is [ˈjestərdeɪz], and 'you' is [juː].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as you would describe a wrong turn.
quests.hint: 'light' and 'left' begin with [l]; 'red' and 'right' begin with [r]. Compare 'light' with 'right'.
quests.explanation: For [l], the tongue tip touches the ridge and air flows around the sides. For [r], the tongue tip pulls back and never touches anything.
quests.textToSpeak: The light was red, so I turned right instead of left.
quests.phoneticHint: 'light' [laɪt] versus 'right' [raɪt]: a brief touch versus no touch. 'left' [left] starts with contact; 'red' [red] starts with the tongue floating.

quests.instruction: Say it twice, slowly and then at natural speed, without blending [l] vs [r].
quests.hint: 'collect' and 'correct' differ only by [l] and [r]. 'library' has both sounds.
quests.explanation: In 'library' the tongue touches for [l], then pulls back for [r]. In 'collect' and 'correct', the first syllable is short and unstressed; the contrast is at the start of the second.
quests.textToSpeak: Did you collect the correct files from the library?
quests.phoneticHint: 'collect' [kəˈlekt], 'correct' [kəˈrekt], and 'library' [ˈlaɪbrəri]. The first [r] in 'library' is not dropped.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as you would describe an apartment.
quests.hint: 'really' has [r] then [l]; 'lovely' has [l], and 'rent' has [r].
quests.explanation: Between [r] and [l] in 'really', the tongue moves from floating to touching. Say each carefully, with the tongue tip only touching the ridge for [l].
quests.textToSpeak: The flat is really lovely, but the rent is too high.
quests.phoneticHint: 'really' is [ˈriːəli] or [ˈrɪli]: [r] first, [l] second. 'flat' [flæt] begins with a quick [fl] cluster.
commonMistakes: Saying both sounds as [l] or both as [r] in 'really'

quests.instruction: Read it aloud and keep the two sounds in [w] vs [v] clearly different.
quests.hint: [w] begins 'we', 'went' and 'waiting'; [v] begins 'visit' and 'vet'. Feel the lips round for one and the teeth touch for the other.
quests.explanation: [w] rounds the lips and never touches the teeth. [v] puts the lower lip against the upper teeth with voice on. Move between them slowly, then at speed.
quests.textToSpeak: We went to visit the vet, but the waiting room was full.
quests.phoneticHint: 'went' [went] versus 'vent' [vent]: lips only versus lip and teeth.
commonMistakes: Not rounding the lips enough for [w]

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a hotel receptionist.
quests.hint: 'would' begins with [w]; 'view' and 'river' contain [v]. Keep them separate.
quests.explanation: 'view' starts [vj]: lip-teeth contact, then a quick [j]. In 'river', the [v] sits between vowels, so keep the lip-teeth contact and voice steady.
quests.textToSpeak: Would you prefer a view of the river or the garden?
quests.phoneticHint: 'view' is [vjuː], 'river' is [ˈrɪvər], and 'would' is [wʊd], with no lip-teeth contact.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a supplier update.
quests.hint: 'twelve' holds both sounds: [w] after [t] and [v] at the end. 'seven' and 'arrived' have [v]; 'Wednesday' and 'we' have [w].
quests.explanation: In 'twelve', the lips round for [w] right after [t], then finish with a voiced [v] at the end, without adding a vowel.
quests.textToSpeak: We ordered twelve, but only seven arrived on Wednesday.
quests.phoneticHint: 'twelve' is [twelv], 'seven' is [ˈsevən], and 'Wednesday' is [ˈwenzdeɪ].

quests.instruction: Read it aloud and keep the two sounds in [b] vs [v] clearly different.
quests.hint: 'berries' begins with [b] and 'very' with [v]. Both have the same vowel after them.
quests.explanation: [b] closes both lips completely, then releases. [v] never fully closes: the lower lip touches the upper teeth while air keeps flowing.
quests.textToSpeak: These berries are very fresh; they came in this morning.
quests.phoneticHint: 'berry' [ˈberi] versus 'very' [ˈveri]: lips stop the air versus lip and teeth let it through.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as you would plan an event.
quests.hint: 'book' and 'bring' begin with [b]; 'venue' begins with [v].
quests.explanation: Notice the different closures: two lips meeting for [b], lip and teeth for [v]. In 'venue', the [v] flows into the vowel with no closure at all.
quests.textToSpeak: Let's book the venue, and I'll bring the drinks.
quests.phoneticHint: 'venue' is [ˈvenjuː]: [v] then a [j] glide near the end; 'book' is [bʊk], with a firm lip closure.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a casual update.
quests.hint: [b] appears in 'been', 'busy' and 'booked'; [v] appears in 'we've', 'very', 'move' and 'haven't'.
quests.explanation: 'move' and 'we've' end with [v], so keep the lip against the teeth to the end. Don't let the sound turn into [b] or vanish.
quests.textToSpeak: We've been very busy with the move, so we haven't even booked a flight.
quests.phoneticHint: 'busy' is [ˈbɪzi], 'booked' is [bʊkt], 'move' is [muːv], and 'haven't' is [ˈhævənt].

quests.instruction: Read it aloud and keep the two sounds in [n] vs [l] clearly different.
quests.hint: 'not', 'and', 'line' and 'moving' contain [n]; 'late' and 'line' contain [l]. 'line' has both.
quests.explanation: Both sounds put the tongue tip on the ridge. For [n], air goes through the nose; for [l], it flows around the sides of the tongue. Pinching the nose only stops [n].
quests.textToSpeak: We're not late, and the line is moving fast.
quests.phoneticHint: 'night' [naɪt] versus 'light' [laɪt]; 'line' [laɪn] starts with [l] and ends with [n].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as you would describe a hotel.
quests.hint: Final [l] closes 'hotel', 'pool' and 'mile'; final [n] closes 'town'.
quests.explanation: Final [l] is a dark sound: the tongue tip lifts while the back of the tongue pulls back. Final [n] keeps the tongue tip on the ridge with air through the nose.
quests.textToSpeak: The hotel has a nice pool, and the town is only a mile away.
quests.phoneticHint: 'mile' [maɪɫ] versus 'mine' [maɪn]; 'town' [taʊn] versus 'towel' [taʊəl].
commonMistakes: Ending 'mile' with [n], so it sounds like 'mine'
Dropping the tongue contact for [l], so 'pool' sounds like 'poo'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a curious question.
quests.hint: 'online' has both [n] and [l]; 'learn' and 'piano' also contain them.
quests.explanation: In 'online', [n] is followed by [l]: the tongue tip stays on the ridge, but the air moves from your nose to the sides of the tongue. Don't add a vowel between them.
quests.textToSpeak: Can you learn to play the piano online?
quests.phoneticHint: 'online' is [ɒnˈlaɪn]: [n], [l], then [n] again. 'learn' [lɜːrn] ends with the tongue tip on the ridge.

quests.instruction: Read it aloud and keep the two sounds in [h] vs no [h] clearly different.
quests.hint: 'hall', 'hard' and 'heat' begin with a breath [h]; 'old' and 'an' begin with vowels only.
quests.explanation: For [h], push a breath through your open mouth before the vowel. Words like 'old' start directly with the vowel, with no breath first.
quests.textToSpeak: It's an old hall, and it's hard to heat.
quests.phoneticHint: 'hall' [hɔːl] versus 'all' [ɔːl]; 'heat' [hiːt] versus 'eat' [iːt].
commonMistakes: Adding [h] to vowel words, so 'old' sounds like 'hold'
Making [h] too harsh, like a throat scrape

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as you would in a stuffy room.
quests.hint: 'heat' and 'heavy' begin with [h]; 'open', 'all', 'awful' and 'air' start with vowels.
quests.explanation: 'the air' is a smooth vowel-to-vowel link, not 'the hair'. Keep the breath out of 'air' and put it back into 'heavy'.
quests.textToSpeak: Open all the windows. The heat is awful, and the air is heavy.
quests.phoneticHint: 'air' [er] versus 'hair' [her]; 'heavy' [ˈhevi] starts with a breathy [h].
commonMistakes: Dropping [h] in 'heavy', so it sounds like 'evy'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a practical suggestion.
quests.hint: The [h] hides inside 'perhaps' and 'rehearse', and begins 'home'.
quests.explanation: In 'perhaps' and 'rehearse', the [h] begins a syllable, so it stays audible even though the word starts with other sounds.
quests.textToSpeak: Perhaps we should rehearse at home before the show.
quests.phoneticHint: 'perhaps' is [pərˈhæps] (often [prˈæps] in fast speech), 'rehearse' is [rɪˈhɜːrs], and 'home' is [hoʊm].
commonMistakes: Dropping the medial [h] in 'rehearse', so it sounds like 'reerse'
Turning the [h] into a hard [k] sound

quests.instruction: Read it aloud and keep the two sounds in [θ] vs [f] clearly different.
quests.hint: 'three' begins with [θ]; 'free' and 'front' begin with [f]. Listen for soft airflow at the teeth versus lip-teeth friction.
quests.explanation: For [θ], the tongue tip rests lightly on the upper teeth; for [f], the lower lip touches the upper teeth. One is tongue, the other is lip.
quests.textToSpeak: There are three free seats near the front.
quests.phoneticHint: 'three' [θriː] versus 'free' [friː]: same vowel and ending, different first sound.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as you would talk about a teacher.
quests.hint: 'taught' begins with [t]; 'theory' and 'thought' begin with [θ].
quests.explanation: For [t], the tongue tip presses on the ridge and blocks the air. For [θ], it rests at the teeth and lets air escape. There is no closure for [θ].
quests.textToSpeak: She taught me the theory, and I thought it made sense.
quests.phoneticHint: 'taught' [tɔːt] versus 'thought' [θɔːt]: nearly identical except for the first sound.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a park worker giving directions.
quests.hint: 'path', 'north' and 'fourth' end with [θ]; 'fourth' also begins with [f].
quests.explanation: At the end of 'path' and 'north', the tongue tip moves to the teeth and lets the air run out. In 'fourth', [θ] follows [r], so the tongue moves forward quickly.
quests.textToSpeak: The path to the north is closed, so use the fourth gate.
quests.phoneticHint: 'fourth' is [fɔːrθ]: [f], vowel, [r], [θ]. 'path' [pæθ] ends softly.
commonMistakes: Dropping the [θ] in 'fourth', so it sounds like 'four'

quests.instruction: Read it aloud and keep the two sounds in [ʒ] clearly different.
quests.hint: 'usually' and 'television' contain [ʒ] in the middle, though no letter 'z' or 'sh' appears.
quests.explanation: [ʒ] is the voiced partner of [ʃ]: pull the tongue back, round the lips, and turn the voice on. In English it only appears in the middle or at the end of words.
quests.textToSpeak: I usually watch television in the evening.
quests.phoneticHint: 'usually' is [ˈjuːʒuəli] and 'television' is [ˈtelɪvɪʒən]. Compare the voiceless [ʃ] in 'Russian' [ˈrʌʃən].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as you would plan a home project.
quests.hint: [ʒ] sits in the middle of 'measure' and, in many accents, at the end of 'garage'.
quests.explanation: In 'measure', [ʒ] comes right after the stressed vowel: make it quick and voiced. Many speakers end 'garage' with [ʒ] too, though [dʒ] is also heard.
quests.textToSpeak: We need to measure the garage before we order the cabinet.
quests.phoneticHint: 'measure' is [ˈmeʒər] and 'garage' is [gəˈrɑːʒ].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a news comment.
quests.hint: 'judge's' and 'village' contain [dʒ]; 'decision' contains [ʒ]. Hear the stop in one and not in the other.
quests.explanation: [dʒ] starts with a tongue closure; [ʒ] is continuous friction. In 'decision', keep the voice going through the [ʒ] and don't add a [d].
quests.textToSpeak: The judge's decision was a surprise to everyone in the village.
quests.phoneticHint: 'judge's' is [ˈdʒʌdʒɪz], 'decision' is [dɪˈsɪʒən], and 'village' is [ˈvɪlɪdʒ].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a bookshop shopper.
quests.hint: 'pick' and 'book' end in [k]; 'bad' ends in [d]; 'big' ends in [g]. Hear the voice stay on in the last two.
quests.explanation: After voiced final stops, the vowel is longer and the voice continues into the closure. After [k], the vowel is shorter and the closure is silent.
quests.textToSpeak: I can't pick a book. This one looks bad, and that one is too big.
quests.phoneticHint: 'bad' [bæd] has a long vowel; 'big' [bɪg]; 'pick' [pɪk] and 'book' [bʊk] end short and crisp.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a warning.
quests.hint: 'leave' ends in [v] and 'prize' in [z], both voiced; 'miss' ends in [s] and 'speech' in [tʃ], both voiceless.
quests.explanation: Voicing at the end of a word signals meaning. Keep the buzz on 'leave' and 'prize' to the very end, and make 'miss' and 'speech' silent hisses.
quests.textToSpeak: If you leave early, you'll miss the prize and the last speech.
quests.phoneticHint: 'leave' [liːv] versus 'leaf' [liːf]; 'prize' [praɪz] versus 'price' [praɪs]; 'miss' [mɪs].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a tech-support complaint.
quests.hint: 'page' ends in voiced [dʒ]; 'search' and 'match' end in voiceless [tʃ].
quests.explanation: Voiced [dʒ] and voiceless [tʃ] use the same tongue movement; only voice and vowel length change. Listen for the difference between 'page' and 'patch'.
quests.textToSpeak: The page keeps crashing when I search for a match.
quests.phoneticHint: 'page' is [peɪdʒ] with a longer diphthong; 'match' is [mætʃ] with a short vowel; 'search' is [sɜːrtʃ].
commonMistakes: Adding a vowel after either sound: 'page-uh'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as you would at a harbour ticket desk.
quests.hint: Three contrasts are in play: [θ] in 'think' and 'three', [ʃ] in 'ship', and [tʃ] in 'check'.
quests.explanation: Keep each tongue position separate: teeth for [θ], a pulled-back hush for [ʃ], a stop-then-hush for [tʃ]. Slow down at 'think', 'ship' and 'check' first.
quests.textToSpeak: The ship leaves at three, I think, so let's check the time.
quests.phoneticHint: 'think' is [θɪŋk], 'ship' is [ʃɪp], 'three' is [θriː], and 'check' is [tʃek].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a friendly question.
quests.hint: [w] begins 'would'; [v] sits in 'live', 'village' and 'river'; [r] is in 'rather' and 'river'; [l] is in 'live' and 'village'.
quests.explanation: Each pair needs a different mouth position: rounded lips for [w], lip-teeth for [v]; a touch for [l], a floating tongue for [r]. Say it slowly first.
quests.textToSpeak: Would you rather live in a village or by the river?
quests.phoneticHint: 'would' [wʊd], 'rather' [ˈræðər], 'live' [lɪv], 'village' [ˈvɪlɪdʒ], 'river' [ˈrɪvər].
commonMistakes: Ending 'live' with [f], so it sounds like 'life'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a scheduling update at work.
quests.hint: 'Thursday' begins with voiceless [θ]; 'the' and 'this' start with voiced [ð]; 'moves' ends in [v]; 'week' and 'Wednesday' begin with [w].
quests.explanation: Both [θ] and [ð] use the tongue at the teeth, but only [ð] buzzes. Round the lips for [w] in 'week' and 'Wednesday', and end 'moves' with a lip-teeth buzz.
quests.textToSpeak: Normally the team meets on Thursday, but this week it moves to Wednesday.
quests.phoneticHint: 'Thursday' is [ˈθɜːrzdeɪ], 'this' is [ðɪs], 'moves' is [muːvz], and 'Wednesday' is [ˈwenzdeɪ].
